verdicts.reason: A: flavor names are set almost as large as the headline and stacked away from their descriptors (Bright & zesty/Warm & herbal/Cool & crisp, also in the wrong order). Two tiny cans are stranded at the bottom right, the bottom-left is empty, and the CTA crowds the logo in the top-right corner. B: a huge CTA sits top-left ahead of the logo, which breaks reading order. The text stack under the single can is cramped, the descriptors are again separated from their names, and the two bottom-left cans are tiny enough to be meaningless. A is marginally better because its can and text still read as product plus copy.

A: the CTA is oversized and placed top-left before the logo. Flavor names and descriptors are stacked in a cramped, mismatched block, and two near-invisible cans sit bottom-left. B: the headline wraps, the flavor names compete with it in size, and the descriptors are separated from their names. Two small cans are orphaned at the bottom right, the 'mixed pack' line collides with a bokeh dot, and the lower half is empty. B keeps a clearer product-to-copy split, so it wins slightly.

Both faithfully keep the original's three-column lineup, hierarchy and CTA block. A clusters the cans within the headline's width, which suits the square canvas and leaves even side margins. B spreads the outer cans wider than the headline, so the grid feels slightly loose against the centered copy. Both leave a bit of dead space at the bottom.

A breaks the design: flavor names compete with the wrapped headline, descriptors are split from their names and out of order, two tiny cans are orphaned at the bottom, and text collides with bokeh dots. B keeps the original structure intact: centered logo, headline, three evenly spaced cans with their labels grouped beneath, then copy, CTA and delivery note in clear order. It needs only minor spacing polish at the bottom.
